So the reasoning denies the antecedent: from "if convicted then barred" it infers "if not convicted then allowed". Choice B.

A concerns the future, but the conclusion is about present eligibility. C says the argument assumes the rule applies only to the audit committee; the argument never limits other committees, and this is not what it needs. D suggests a confusion between convictions that the argument does not make. E says the chairperson relies on opinion, but the chairperson relies on the rule.
questions.tip: "If A then not-B" does not give "if not A then B". A bar on one condition does not guarantee everything else.
questions.trap: A sounds practical, but eligibility now is what is at stake. The deeper flaw is logical: the rule excludes; it does not include.

questions.prompt:
Every morning, the tea stall near the metro station sells out of samosas by 9 am. The owner says that he bakes the same number of samosas each day, and that the number of customers has grown steadily for months. If that trend continues, therefore, __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the stall will soon have to close
customers prefer samosas to every other snack the stall sells
the metro station will soon become busier at every hour of the day
the owner should raise the price of a samosa
he will sell out of samosas even earlier in the morning unless he makes more of them
questions.explanation:
"Therefore" tells you the blank is a conclusion, so it must follow from the facts given: a fixed supply of samosas, a growing number of customers, and a stall that already sells out. If demand grows and supply stays fixed, the stock will run out sooner, unless supply rises. That is choice E.

A is far too strong; selling out is a sign of demand, not trouble. B compares samosas with other snacks, but nothing is said about other snacks. C claims the station is busier at all hours; the passage only speaks of customers at this stall. D recommends an action; nothing in the facts shows that raising the price is the natural next step.
questions.tip: For a "therefore" blank, restate the facts in one line and ask: what must follow?
questions.trap: D: a sensible business idea is not the same as a logical consequence of the stated facts.

questions.prompt:
Mehra Textiles buys its dye from Supplier A. A new company, Supplier B, has offered to supply dye in the same range of shades, and Mehra's chemists have confirmed that the two products are identical in colour fastness. Mehra should switch to Supplier B, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: Supplier A has supplied Mehra for many years
Supplier B is based in a different state from Supplier A
dye is only one of several materials that Mehra buys
many textile firms use more than one dye supplier
Supplier B's dye costs less per litre than Supplier A's
questions.explanation:
The blank follows "because", so it needs a reason to switch. The passage has already shown that the two dyes match in shades and fastness, so the only thing left that could favour B is something like price. E supplies it.

A is a reason to stay with A. B is a fact about location that does not show an advantage. C says dye is one of several purchases, which, if anything, reduces its importance. D describes what other firms do, which gives no reason that applies to Mehra's choice.
questions.tip: For a "because" blank, ask what advantage is still missing once the equalities have been stated.
questions.trap: A supports the opposite recommendation.

questions.prompt:
In a survey of 400 commuters in Pune, most of those who cycle to work said they started cycling after the city opened its protected cycle lanes. A smaller group said they already cycled but now do so more often. Nobody said they had given up cycling since the lanes opened. The survey's authors conclude that __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: every commuter who lives near a protected lane now cycles to work
the protected lanes appear to have encouraged more commuters to cycle to work
cycling is now the most common way to commute in Pune
the protected lanes have reduced traffic congestion in the city
cycling to work makes commuters healthier than other commuters
questions.explanation:
Look for the claim that the survey results directly support. Most cyclists began after the lanes opened, some cycle more, and no one quit. All of that points towards the lanes encouraging cycling: B. The hedge "appear to" keeps the claim within what a survey can show.

A goes much further than the evidence: "every commuter" is far too strong. C compares cycling with other modes of commuting, but the survey gives no figures for them. D talks about congestion, which was not surveyed. E is a health claim, and health is not mentioned.
questions.tip: Conclusion blanks should not outrun the premises. Watch for "every", "most common" and other claims the data never mention.
questions.trap: D: a familiar benefit of cycle lanes in the real world, but not something this survey tested.

questions.prompt:
Tiruvella Hospital is a large public hospital that serves several districts. Tiruvella Hospital plans to move visiting hours from the afternoon to the evening. At present, doctors' ward rounds take place in the afternoon. The hospital's administrators argue that the change will reduce the number of delayed rounds, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: families generally prefer to visit in the evening
senior doctors are the ones who decide when ward rounds begin
the hospital has more patients this year than last year
visitors arriving in the afternoon currently crowd the wards and hold up the doctors' rounds
the hospital has fewer nurses on duty in the evening than in the afternoon
questions.explanation:
The blank follows "because" and must explain why moving visiting hours reduces delays to rounds. The link is that visitors and rounds currently happen at the same time. If visitors crowd the wards and delay doctors, moving visits to the evening removes the clash. Choice D supplies that bridge.

A might explain why families would welcome the change, but it says nothing about the doctors' rounds. B explains who sets the schedule, but not why visitors would delay it. C is a general fact about patient numbers, with no link to delays. E adds a possible downside of evening visits; it could harm the plan but does not support it.
questions.tip: A good "because" choice connects the two things named in the claim; here, visiting hours and delayed rounds.
questions.trap: A sounds like a good reason to change visiting hours, but the sentence is about delayed rounds.

questions.prompt:
Researchers had two groups of adult learners study the same 140 minutes of a new language over one week. One group studied for 20 minutes every day; the other studied for a single 140-minute session. A month later, the first group remembered far more. The researchers conclude that what matters for retention is not the total time spent studying but __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: which language is being studied
the age of the learner
how that time is spread over the days of the week
whether the study takes place in the morning
the number of words in the textbook
questions.explanation:
The phrase "not X but ___" signals a contrast. X (total time) was equalised, since both groups studied 140 minutes. The only difference between the groups was how the time was distributed. So the answer must name that factor: C.

A, B and E refer to features that were the same for both groups or that the passage never mentions. D names a possible factor, but the two groups' study times of day are not described as different; the actual difference was daily spreading versus a single session.
questions.tip: In "not X but ___" blanks, look for what the passage varied between the groups while holding X constant.
questions.trap: D: plausible in real life, but the experiment did not vary it.

questions.prompt:
A city measured air pollution at two monitoring stations: one beside a major highway and one in a park two kilometres away. Over a year, the highway station's readings averaged three times those of the park station. During three weeks when the highway was closed for repairs, the readings at the two stations were nearly equal. Therefore, __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: most of the pollution recorded at the highway station is probably due to traffic on the highway
the park is entirely free of pollution from any source
closing the highway permanently would remove all pollution from the highway station's readings
pollution at the park station comes mainly from wind blowing from the highway
pollution levels in the city as a whole are rising
questions.explanation:
The blank follows "Therefore", so it is the conclusion. Compare the two conditions: with the highway open the readings differ by a factor of three, with it closed they are nearly equal. So the extra pollution at the highway station disappears when the highway traffic stops. The natural conclusion is A.

B claims zero pollution at the park; the park's readings are not zero, they are just equal to the highway station's during the closure. C is too strong: "all" pollution would not be removed, since there is a baseline that the park also records. D contradicts the data: if wind carried the highway's pollution to the park, the stations would not have become equal when the highway closed. E is about trends over time, which the passage does not give.
questions.tip: When a difference vanishes as soon as one condition is removed, the removed condition probably explains the difference.
questions.trap: C attaches to the right idea but overstates it ("all", "permanently").

questions.prompt:
A publisher plans to raise its e-book prices, arguing that sales will not fall because readers who buy e-books value convenience. A survey of e-book readers found, however, that most of them also borrow e-books free from public libraries, and that they would simply borrow more if prices rose. The price rise would therefore reduce the publisher's e-book sales, unless __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the publisher also sells printed books through bookshops
convenience is the main reason that readers choose e-books over print
libraries have such long waiting lists for the publisher's titles that readers who cannot wait would still buy them
public libraries buy their e-book licences from the publisher
rival publishers charge higher prices for e-books than this publisher does
questions.explanation:
"Unless" asks for a condition that removes the threat. The threat is that readers will switch to library borrowing. Anything that makes borrowing a poor substitute would remove it. Long waiting lists do that: readers who want a book now would still pay. Choice C.

A concerns printed books, so it does not affect e-book sales. B repeats the publisher's own claim, which the survey has already challenged: it gives no reason why readers would not borrow instead. D is true-sounding but does not change the fact that a borrowed copy is not a sale. E is about rivals, but readers' alternative here is borrowing, not rival publishers.
questions.tip: With "unless", name the threat first, then find the choice that disarms it.
questions.trap: B: it looks like a defence of the publisher, but it is the same claim that the survey has already undercut.

questions.prompt:
A school wants to cut the time students spend queuing for lunch. Observers found that the queue forms at the payment desk, where a single cashier handles all students, while the serving counter moves quickly. The school should therefore add a second payment desk rather than a second serving counter, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the school's lunch break is only 40 minutes long
most students bring packed lunches on Fridays
the serving counter is located next to the school entrance
students at other schools spend less time queuing for lunch
extra capacity shortens a queue only at the step that limits how fast students can get through
questions.explanation:
The blank follows "because" and has to justify putting the new capacity at the payment desk rather than the serving counter. The passage says the queue forms at the payment desk; that is the bottleneck. The principle that links this to the recommendation is that adding capacity helps where flow is limited. That is E.

A adds urgency but does not choose between the desk and the counter. B is about a different group of students and a particular day. C says where the counter is, which has no bearing on where capacity is needed. D compares with other schools but does not say why the payment desk is the place to add capacity.
questions.tip: A strong "because" choice is the principle that makes the observation lead to the recommendation.
questions.trap: A: it supports "do something about queues", which the passage has already taken for granted.

questions.prompt:
A regional museum has been experimenting with a new approach to its exhibitions. A museum's new exhibition has drawn 30 percent more visitors than the exhibition it replaced. Admission prices are unchanged, and the museum's advertising budget was cut by a quarter when the exhibition opened. Therefore, __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: whatever accounts for the increase in visitors, it is not an increase in the museum's spending on advertising
the new exhibition is entirely responsible for the increase in visitors
advertising has no effect on attendance at museums
attendance at the museum will keep rising next year
the museum's other exhibitions are less popular than the new one
questions.explanation:
"Therefore" calls for a conclusion that follows from what we have been told. The advertising budget fell, yet visitors rose. So an increase in advertising spending cannot be the explanation. That is the safest conclusion, and it is A.

B goes too far: the exhibition may be a cause, but other factors (the season, a festival, a school visit scheme) are not ruled out. C generalises from one museum to every museum, and even here advertising may help; the claim is only that it did not drive this rise. D predicts the future; nothing supports it. E compares exhibitions, and no data about the others are given.
questions.tip: The strongest conclusions are often negative and modest: "it cannot be X".
questions.trap: B: it says the new exhibition is the whole story, which is what you would like to be true but cannot be shown.

questions.prompt:
A national trade group and a leading economist have been debating a proposed import ban. A trade group argues that banning imported steel would protect jobs in the country's steel mills. An economist replies that the ban would nevertheless reduce total employment, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: some industries that use steel would face higher costs and might cut a few jobs
imported steel is, on average, cheaper than domestic steel
the steel mills are located mainly in regions where unemployment is high
many industries that use steel would face higher costs and would lay off more workers than the mills would save
steel imports have been falling for several years
questions.explanation:
The economist's claim is about total employment, so the blank must show that the jobs lost outweigh the jobs saved. Only D does this: it names a mechanism (higher input costs for steel-using industries) and states that the resulting layoffs exceed the jobs saved in the mills.

A is the closest decoy. It names the same mechanism but says only "some" industries and "a few jobs", which does not show that the total falls. B gives a cost fact, but without linking it to jobs elsewhere. C supports the trade group's case, since it adds to the value of protecting mill jobs. E suggests the ban would matter less, but it does not show any job loss.
questions.tip: When a claim is about a total or net effect, the supporting premise must compare gains and losses.
questions.trap: A: right mechanism, wrong strength. A "because" reason must be strong enough to carry the conclusion.

questions.prompt:
Studies show that employees who work from home at least two days a week report higher job satisfaction than those who work wholly in the office. However, employees choose their arrangements, and those who most value flexibility are the likeliest to seek roles that allow home working. A company is considering requiring all its employees to work from home two days a week. On the basis of the studies, the company can conclude only that __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the requirement would raise the satisfaction of every employee
the studies do not show that the requirement would raise satisfaction among employees who would not have chosen to work from home
working from home lowers productivity even as it raises satisfaction
most employees would prefer to work from home two days a week
satisfaction depends more on flexibility than on pay
questions.explanation:
The stimulus supplies a crucial warning: the people in the studies chose home working, so they may differ from employees who did not. The company plans to apply the arrangement to everyone, including people who would not have chosen it. So the only safe conclusion is that the studies do not show that satisfaction would rise for such employees. Choice B.

A claims a universal benefit, which the studies cannot support. C adds a claim about productivity that is not in the studies. D claims what employees prefer, but no preference survey of the whole workforce is given. E compares flexibility with pay, and pay is not discussed.
questions.tip: "Can conclude only that" asks for the modest, defensible claim, often a statement of what the evidence does not show.
questions.trap: D: if people who chose home working are happier, it is tempting to say most people would want it, but the people studied were self-selected.

questions.prompt:
A team of archaeologists has spent three seasons excavating a bronze-age settlement. Its houses were built of stone and mud brick, and the site shows no sign of fire or violent destruction. Few settlements of the period have been excavated so thoroughly. Archaeologists argue that a bronze-age settlement was abandoned suddenly rather than gradually, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: no weapons were found anywhere on the site
household goods, including tools and stored grain, were found where they would have been in daily use, with no sign that the occupants had packed up
the settlement lay beside a river that later changed course
tree-ring records show a severe drought in the region in the decade before
the settlement was larger than any other of the same period in the area
questions.explanation:
The claim is about how the abandonment happened: suddenly. The strongest support would be evidence of people leaving without time to pack or take their possessions. Tools and stored grain left in place show exactly that: B.

A tells us nothing about the way people left. C could explain why they left but not whether they left suddenly or slowly. D suggests a cause, and a drought that built over a decade would, if anything, suggest a gradual decline. E compares size, which is irrelevant to how the departure occurred.
questions.tip: Match the "because" reason to the exact claim: evidence about why something happened does not show how quickly.
questions.trap: C and D explain why people might leave; the claim is about speed.

questions.prompt:
Among the world's fifty largest cities, those that introduced congestion charges saw average travel times fall by 10 percent over three years, while cities without such charges saw travel times rise by 5 percent. Almost all of the cities that introduced charges also expanded their public transport networks substantially during the same three years; few of the other cities did. On the basis of these figures alone, the most that can be concluded is that __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: congestion charges alone reduce travel times by about 10 percent
expanding public transport has no effect on travel times unless it is paired with congestion charges
cities that introduce congestion charges will see travel times fall within three years
the data do not separate the effect of congestion charges from the effect of expanded public transport on travel times
congestion charges and public transport expansion have equal effects on travel times
questions.explanation:
"The most that can be concluded" asks for the claim that the evidence supports, and no more. Two things changed together in the same cities: congestion charges and public transport expansion. Travel times improved in those cities, but because the two changes coincided almost completely, the figures cannot say how much belongs to each. That is D.

A gives all the credit to the charges. B is a stronger claim than the data allow; it says public transport is useless on its own, but the data say nothing about transport expansion alone. C makes a prediction for any city, which these figures cannot support, given the confounded changes. E claims equal effects, but the figures cannot show the size of either.
questions.tip: When two changes occur together, the evidence cannot tell you which one (or what mix) produced the result.
questions.trap: A treats the headline figure (10 percent) as the effect of the charge; the 10 percent belongs to the bundle of changes.

questions.prompt:
In a clinical trial, the average improvement in the group taking a new drug was the same as the average improvement in the group taking a placebo. The company's data show, however, that in the drug group a large number of patients improved a great deal while many others got slightly worse. In the placebo group, nearly all patients improved by modest and similar amounts. The company should therefore not conclude that the drug is useless, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: placebos are known to produce improvement in a proportion of patients
the drug group and the placebo group were each large enough to give a stable average
the average improvement in both groups was modest
the patients in the drug group who got worse did so by chance
an average equal to the placebo's can result from large benefits for some patients that are offset by small harms to others, in which case the drug may help an identifiable subgroup
questions.explanation:
The conclusion to be defended is "the drug is not useless". The key facts are that the averages match but the spread differs: some drug patients improved a lot, some got slightly worse. The reason must show that equal averages do not mean no benefit. E does so: a large gain for some can cancel a small loss for others and leave the average the same as a placebo's, while still pointing to a group that benefits.

A is about the placebo effect, which explains the placebo group's gain but not why the drug could still be useful. B speaks of sample size, which would make the average more reliable and so would support the view that the drug does no better than placebo. C is a description of the averages and does not help to show that the drug has value. D is unsupported; the passage does not say the worsening was due to chance, and even if so, it would not explain the large improvements.
questions.tip: An average hides the distribution. Equal averages can mask very different spreads.
questions.trap: B: "big, reliable groups" sounds scientific and pro-evidence, but it would reinforce the view that the drug is equivalent to a placebo on average.

questions.prompt:
A stationery shop in a coastal town keeps careful records of its daily sales. Every day last monsoon month on which it rained, the stationery shop sold out of umbrellas by noon. It rained on 12 days that month. Therefore, __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the shop sold out of umbrellas by noon on at least 12 days that month
the shop sold out of umbrellas by noon on exactly 12 days that month
the shop sells umbrellas only when it rains
the shop should order more umbrellas for next month
it rained more that month than in any previous month
questions.explanation:
"Therefore" asks for a conclusion that follows. On each rainy day the shop sold out by noon. There were 12 rainy days, so there were at least 12 such days. We cannot rule out additional sell-outs on dry days, so "at least" is the safe wording. Choice A.

B says "exactly", but the passage says nothing about dry days. C claims umbrellas sell only in rain, which is not stated. D gives advice, which is not a logical consequence. E compares with earlier months; no earlier data are given.
questions.tip: Watch the difference between "at least" and "exactly": premises about some cases rarely fix an exact total.
questions.trap: B: swapping "at least" for "exactly" is a tiny change that makes the claim unsupported.

questions.prompt:
Opposition economists have questioned the finance ministry's latest pension proposals. The finance ministry says that raising the retirement age will cut the pension deficit. But raising the retirement age will not necessarily reduce the deficit, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: pension deficits exist in many other countries
the retirement age was last raised ten years ago
older workers who are kept in employment may claim disability benefits that the state would otherwise not pay, offsetting the pension savings
some people choose to retire earlier than the official age
people now live longer than they did a generation ago
questions.explanation:
The blank follows "because" and must give a reason why the saving might not materialise. C offers a mechanism: the money saved on pensions could be spent on other benefits. That directly attacks "will reduce the deficit".

A is a fact about other countries and has no bearing on this one. B gives a date but no mechanism. D may be true, yet early retirement is already part of today's pension costs and does not show that the saving fails. E gives a reason that actually makes pensions costlier and so supports raising the age.
questions.tip: Premise blanks that say "not necessarily" need a specific mechanism, not just a general doubt.
questions.trap: E: it is about pensions and retirement, so it feels on topic, but it supports the opposite side.

questions.prompt:
Residents of a town have been arguing over a proposed flyover in the town centre, and the council recently circulated a survey on the subject. The local newspaper argues that the council's survey of residents' views on the new flyover cannot be trusted, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the survey was sent only to households that had previously written to the council, and such households are likely to hold stronger views than others
the flyover is being built by a private contractor
the council has run many surveys on many subjects
the survey asked about the flyover and about nothing else
the survey cost more than the council had budgeted
questions.explanation:
The claim is that the survey cannot be trusted as a measure of residents' views. The best reason is one that makes the sample unrepresentative: only households that had already written to the council received it. People who write to councils are not a typical cross-section. Choice A.

B is about who builds the flyover, not about the survey's reliability. C says the council runs surveys often, which is not a reason to distrust this one. D describes a focused survey, which, if anything, is a good feature. E concerns cost, not accuracy.
questions.tip: To doubt a survey, point to who answered, how they were chosen, or how the question was put.
questions.trap: E: a council that overspends invites criticism, but cost does not make the results less reliable.

questions.prompt:
All 40 employees who attended the company's workshop passed the certification exam. Only employees who have passed the certification exam are eligible for promotion. Several employees who did not attend the workshop also passed the certification exam. Therefore, __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: all of the employees who attended the workshop will be promoted
the workshop is the only route to passing the certification exam
attending the workshop is not a requirement for passing the certification exam
employees who did not attend the workshop are more likely to be promoted
passing the certification exam guarantees that an employee will be promoted
questions.explanation:
The facts: all attendees passed; some non-attendees passed; passing is required for promotion eligibility. The firm conclusion available is that you can pass without attending, which is C.

A treats passing as enough for promotion. The passage says passing is needed (only those who have passed are eligible), not that it is enough. B is contradicted by the non-attendees who passed. D is a claim about likelihood that the facts do not support. E is the same necessary-versus-sufficient mistake as A.
questions.tip: "Only those who X are eligible" makes X necessary, not sufficient.
questions.trap: A and E: they upgrade a requirement into a guarantee.

questions.prompt:
In one region, a dry year occurs about one year in five. In a dry year, a new seed yields 90 units per plot, while the standard seed yields 40 units. In a normal year, the new seed yields 85 units per plot and the standard seed 100 units. Therefore, a farmer who plants only the new seed over a typical five-year period will __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: harvest much less in total than a farmer who plants only the standard seed
harvest slightly less in total than a farmer who plants only the standard seed
harvest more in total than a farmer who plants only the standard seed
lose the entire crop in the dry year
harvest exactly the same total as a farmer who plants only the standard seed
questions.explanation:
Compute the five-year totals for a typical period: one dry year and four normal years. New seed: 90 + 4 × 85 = 90 + 340 = 430. Standard seed: 40 + 4 × 100 = 40 + 400 = 440. So the new seed gives 10 units less (about 2 percent). That is "slightly less": B.

A overstates the gap, which is small. C would be true if you counted only the dry year, where the new seed does far better (90 versus 40). D contradicts the data: it yields 90 in a dry year. E is the tempting result of expecting the two benefits to cancel exactly.
questions.tip: Do the weighted arithmetic: dry-year gain (+50) is outweighed by four normal-year losses (−15 each, −60).
questions.trap: C: focusing on the dramatic dry-year advantage and forgetting that normal years are four times as common.

questions.prompt:
While the number of tourists visiting the city rose 25 percent over five years, hotel revenue rose only 10 percent. An analyst argues that this gap reflects a change in the type of tourist rather than any decline in the quality of the city's hotels, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: hotel room prices rose by about 10 percent over the same five years
hotel occupancy in the city is high in every season
hotels in other cities showed similar revenue growth over the period
tourists spend more on food and shopping than they do on accommodation
most of the additional tourists were day-trippers and budget travellers who spend little or nothing on hotel rooms
questions.explanation:
The analyst says the gap comes from the kind of tourist, not hotel quality. The reason that fits is that the extra tourists spend little on hotels: E. That would explain why more tourists did not mean proportionally more hotel revenue.

A is a pricing fact; with prices up 10 percent and revenue up 10 percent, it would suggest the number of room-nights sold did not grow at all, but it does not say anything about the type of tourist or about quality. B says occupancy is high, which would suggest more visitors should yield more revenue, deepening the puzzle. C shows other cities are similar, which is not an explanation about tourist type in this city. D compares categories of spending, which does not show why hotel revenue lagged.
questions.tip: Choose the reason that explains the specific gap and fits the analyst's chosen explanation (here, "type of tourist").
questions.trap: A: numbers match (10 percent), so it looks like a neat explanation, but it neither addresses tourist type nor ruled out quality.

questions.prompt:
Brand Z, once a market leader in packaged snacks, has seen its sales fall for four years in a row. Brand Z's marketing director has asked for a bigger advertising budget to revive the brand's sales. A consultant replies that no amount of advertising will help Brand Z, because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: Brand Z's advertising budget is smaller than those of its main rivals
Brand Z's current advertisements are poorly designed
Brand Z has a smaller share of the market than its main rivals
nearly all potential customers already know the brand, and most of those who have tried it say they would not buy it again
advertising is expensive compared with other marketing activities
questions.explanation:
"No amount of advertising will help" is a strong claim. To support it, the reason must show that what advertising can do (raise awareness, draw first-time buyers) is not what Brand Z lacks, and that its real problem is something advertising cannot fix. D does exactly this: awareness is already high, and people who try the product don't repeat the purchase.

A and B each suggest that better or more advertising could help, which supports the marketing director. C describes the problem but does not explain why advertising could not cure it. E says advertising is costly, which is not the same as saying it cannot help.
questions.tip: When the claim says "no amount of X will work", the reason must show X addresses a problem the brand does not have.
questions.trap: E: "expensive" is an argument against spending a lot, not against its ever working.

questions.prompt:
A survey of 100 farmers in a village found that 70 own a tractor and 60 own an irrigation pump. A district officer who is planning a subsidy for farmers who own both machines claims that some surveyed farmers will qualify immediately. The claim is justified because __________.

Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: most farmers who own a tractor also own a pump
pump owners outnumber tractor owners in the village
tractor owners tend to be wealthier than other farmers
the number of tractor owners and pump owners together exceeds the number of farmers surveyed, so the two groups must overlap
the subsidy is meant to go to farmers who already own both machines
questions.explanation:
Pure counting: 70 + 60 = 130, which is more than the 100 farmers. If the groups did not overlap, there would have to be 130 farmers. So at least 130 − 100 = 30 own both. That is exactly the justification: D.

A is not supported. At least 30 of the 70 tractor owners must own a pump, which could be as few as 43 percent, not "most". B is contradicted by the numbers (60 pump owners versus 70 tractor owners). C is an unsupported claim about wealth. E is about the purpose of the subsidy and has nothing to do with whether any farmer qualifies.
questions.tip: For two overlapping groups in a fixed population: minimum overlap = (A + B) − total.
questions.trap: A: if the groups overlap, it feels natural to say "most" do both, but the arithmetic only gives a minimum of 30.
